Your task is to generate a complete research paper using the materials below.
You must produce:
1. A BibTeX bibliography file (references.bib)
2. The full LaTeX paper (template.tex)

Instructions
• Use the research idea and experimental logs to construct a coherent, rigorous ML paper.
• For related work and baselines:
  – Search for and include influential papers published up until 2024-10.
  – Incorporate relevant literature and add the corresponding BibTeX entries to references.bib.
  – Do NOT hallucinate papers or reference keys; all citation entries must be real.
• In the LaTeX paper, cite papers using \cite{} with keys that match exactly with your entries in references.bib.
• Do not fabricate experimental results or make claims unsupported by the logs.

Materials
Here are all the raw research materials to assist with the writing process:

[RESEARCH IDEA]
## Problem Statement
Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) currently suffer from a critical reliability issue known as "object hallucination," where the model generates descriptions containing non-existent objects or misrepresents existing ones. While current mitigation strategies involve resource-intensive fine-tuning or external detection modules, these approaches often face scalability issues or fail to fully exploit the intrinsic visual information within the model. A significant cause of this hallucination is the model's inability to resolve fine-grained details when processing a single global image, as irrelevant background objects distract the attention mechanism and low resolution obscures critical visual features.

## Core Hypothesis
We hypothesize that we can significantly mitigate object hallucination by dynamically re-focusing the model's attention on high-resolution local regions during the generation process.

Our intuition is twofold:
1.  **Resolution & Distraction:** Splitting an image into sub-images removes visual noise (unnecessary objects) and increases the effective resolution of the target objects.
2.  **Self-Correction via Attention:** The model's own internal attention maps indicate *where* it is trying to look. We can use this signal to weight the contribution of specific sub-images, ensuring the generated text is grounded in the most relevant, high-clarity visual data at each decoding step.

## Proposed Methodology (High-Level Technical Approach)

We propose **Ensemble Decoding (ED)**, a training-free inference strategy that intervenes in the decoding loop to fuse global context with local details.

**1. Multi-View Input Strategy**
Instead of a single forward pass, we will partition the input image into a grid of overlapping sub-images. We will feed the model a set of inputs comprising the original "global" image and these "local" sub-images simultaneously.

**2. Dynamic Attention-Guided Weighting**
At every step of token generation, we will extract the model's self-attention maps. We aim to interpret these maps to determine which specific sub-image the model is focusing on for the current concept.
*   We will aggregate attention scores within the regions corresponding to each sub-image.
*   These scores will be normalized to create a dynamic weight vector, assigning higher importance to the sub-image that aligns with the model's current visual focus.

**3. Logit Ensemble and Aggregation**
We will perform parallel inference on the global and local inputs. The final output probability distribution (logits) for the next token will be a weighted ensemble of the logits from all inputs. The global image provides context, while the attention-weighted sub-images provide high-resolution details.

**4. Adaptive Plausibility Constraint**
Simply averaging logits might dilute sharp, fine-grained predictions. To prevent this, we will introduce a filtering mechanism (an adaptive constraint) that calibrates the distribution. This ensures that only tokens that are plausible across the weighted consensus of views are considered, suppressing hallucinations derived from low-confidence noise.

**5. Efficiency Optimization (FastED)**
To address the computational overhead of processing multiple image crops, we will design an optimized variant. Instead of calculating full logits for *all* sub-images at every step, this variant will use the attention map to select only the single most relevant sub-image (the "winner") to combine with the global view, reducing the required forward passes.

## Expected Contribution
*   **Training-Free Mitigation:** A plug-and-play decoding strategy that reduces hallucination without requiring parameter updates or external datasets.
*   **Enhanced Visual Grounding:** A mechanism that effectively utilizes high-resolution local features to correct the model's tendency to drift, validating the importance of resolution and attention focus in LVLM reliability.
*   **Dynamic Visual Adaptability:** A framework where the model dynamically selects its visual source (global vs. specific local crop) token-by-token, mirroring human visual scanning behavior.

[EXPERIMENTAL LOGS]
## 1. Experimental Setup

We utilized a specific set of configurations, datasets, and metrics to evaluate the proposed Ensemble Decoding (ED) and FastED strategies against baseline methods.

*   **Base Model:** LLaVA-1.5 (7B and 13B parameters) utilizing a patch-wise projector.
*   **Datasets:**
    *   **POPE (Polling-based Object Probing Evaluation):** Includes 27,000 Yes/No questions across MSCOCO, A-OKVQA, and GQA datasets. Splits include Random, Popular, and Adversarial settings (balanced 50% existent/non-existent).
    *   **CHAIR (Caption Hallucination Assessment with Image Relevance):** subset of 100 randomly selected images from MSCOCO.
    *   **MME:** Hallucination subset evaluated on four subtasks: Existence, Count, Position, and Color.
    *   **LLaVA-Bench:** 24 images and 60 questions assessing complex tasks and domain adaptation.
*   **Evaluation Metrics:**
    *   **POPE:** Precision, Recall, F1 Score, Accuracy.
    *   **CHAIR:** CHAIRs (sentence-level hallucination), CHAIRi (instance-level hallucination), Recall, Average Length.
    *   **MME:** Accuracy and Accuracy+.
    *   **LLaVA-Bench:** GPT-4 aided evaluation scoring Accuracy and Detailedness on a 1-10 Likert scale.
    *   **Efficiency:** Inference Latency (average time per image).
*   **Baselines Compared:**
    *   **Regular:** Multinomial sampling decoding.
    *   **VCD:** Visual Contrastive Decoding.
    *   **DoLA:** Decoding by Contrasting Layers.
    *   **OPERA:** Over-Trust Penalty and Retrospection-Allocation.
    *   **AGLA:** Assembly of Global and Local Attention.
*   **Implementation Details:**
    *   **Image Splitting:** Input images were split into $N = 4$ sub-images.
    *   **Sub-image Size:** 336 × 336 pixels.
    *   **Overlap Strategy:** Images with width/height exceeding 672 pixels were resized to 448 × 448 before splitting to ensure overlap.
    *   **Hyperparameters:**
        *   Weighted term $\alpha = 0.5$.
        *   Truncation strength $\beta = 0.5$.
        *   Softmax temperature $\tau$: 1e-2 for short-answer tasks (POPE, MME), 1e-4 for long-answer tasks (CHAIR, LLaVA-Bench).
    *   **Attention Mechanism:** Top $H = 3$ heads and top $K = 3$ layers were selected.
    *   **Hardware:** Experiments conducted on a single A6000 GPU.
    *   **Replication:** All experiments were repeated three times; reported results are averaged.

## 3. Qualitative Observations

**Pilot Study Findings:**
*   Observation: We manipulated image variables using grid-arranged images.
*   Observation: Masking 1/4 of irrelevant areas improved model performance.
*   Observation: Lowering object resolution caused performance to decline, a trend that worsened as the number of objects increased.
*   Conclusion: Sub-images help the model attend to relevant objects by containing fewer irrelevant objects and maintaining higher resolution.

**MME Benchmark Analysis:**
*   Observation: ED achieved the highest performance on Position and Color-related questions in the hallucination subset.
*   Observation: ED achieved near-perfect accuracy on Existence-related questions.
*   Observation: ED performance was lower on Object Counting tasks compared to Existence/Position, attributed to image splitting fragmenting objects.

**LLaVA-Bench Analysis:**
*   Observation: Both FastED and ED outperformed Regular decoding and the AGLA baseline in GPT-aided evaluations.
*   Observation: ED demonstrated a significant improvement in the "Detailedness" score compared to FastED.
*   Observation: FastED performed slightly better than ED in "Accuracy" on LLaVA-Bench in the main bar chart comparison, though ED remained superior to baselines.

**Qualitative Output Analysis:**
*   Observation: In comparative examples, Regular and AGLA methods generated hallucinations (e.g., describing a "bench" or "boat" not present in the image).
*   Observation: AGLA's static masking failed to update during token generation, limiting fine detail description.
*   Observation: ED generated dynamic attention maps at each token generation step (e.g., attending to "wooden," "snow-capped," "calm"), successfully avoiding hallucinations found in baselines.

**Ablation Study Observations:**
*   **APC vs. ED APC:** When comparing the general Adaptive Plausibility Constraint (APC) to the proposed ED APC, both yielded identical results at $\beta=0$. However, as $\beta$ increased, ED APC consistently outperformed standard APC.
*   **Model Size:** ED consistently outperformed Regular decoding across both 7B and 13B model sizes on POPE. The 13B ED model generally achieved higher performance than the 7B ED model.

**GPT-Aided Case Studies (Specific Examples):**
*   **Case 1 (Regular vs ED):** Regular described a "creepy sculpture of a pig" with "flames from ears". ED correctly described a "fire-breathing lizard statue" with glasses. GPT-4 scored ED higher (Acc: 8, Detail: 6) vs Regular (Acc: 2, Detail: 4).
*   **Case 2 (Regular vs FastED):** Regular misidentified lobster as "crayfish" and hallucinated the count (5 vs 4). FastED correctly identified lobster and seasoning details. GPT-4 scored FastED higher (Acc: 9, Detail: 8) vs Regular (Acc: 6, Detail: 7).

Conference Guidelines
# ICLR 2025 Paper Writing Guidelines

Below are the instructions to help you with the LaTeX paper writing process for ICLR 2025.

## General Setup
* **Document Class:** `\documentclass{article}`
* **Required Packages:**
    ```latex
    \usepackage{iclr2025_conference,times}
    \usepackage{hyperref}
    \usepackage{url}
    % Optional but recommended for math
    \input{math_commands.tex}
    ```
* **Style Files:** You must use `iclr2025_conference.sty` and `iclr2025_conference.bst`.

## Anonymity (Crucial)
* ICLR is double-blind. **Do not** include real author names or affiliations in the submission version, use "Ambitious AI Researcher" instead.
* Use the third person when citing your own prior work (e.g., "Earlier work by Smalle (2024)..." instead of "In our earlier work...").
* You may post your paper on arXiv, but do not explicitly refer to the arXiv version in the paper to maintain anonymity.

## Paper Length
* **Main Text:** Strict upper limit of **10 pages**.
* **Citations:** Unlimited additional pages.
* **Ethics & Reproducibility Statements:** Optional. Do not count toward the page limit (max 1 page each).
* **Acknowledgments:** Do not count toward the page limit.

## Abstract
The abstract must be limited to **one paragraph**.
* **Margins:** Indented 1/2 inch (3 picas) on both left and right-hand margins.
* **Font:** 10-point type, vertical spacing of 11-points.
* **Title:** The word `\textsc{Abstract}` must be centered, in small caps, and in point size 12.
* **Spacing:** Two line spaces precede the abstract.

## Formatting Your Paper
The text must be confined within a rectangle 5.5 inches (33 picas) wide and 9 inches (54 picas) long. The left margin is 1.5 inch (9 picas).
* **Font:** Times New Roman (via `times` package) is preferred.
* **Size:** 10-point type with 11-point vertical spacing.
* **Paragraphs:** Separated by 1/2 line space, with **no indentation**.
* **Paper Title:** 17-point, small caps, left-aligned.

### Headings
* **First Level:** Small caps (`\textsc`), flush left, 12-point. One line space before, 1/2 after.
* **Second Level:** Small caps, flush left, 10-point. One line space before, 1/2 after.
* **Third Level:** Small caps, flush left, 10-point. One line space before, 1/2 after.

## Citations and References
Use the `natbib` package (loaded automatically by the style file).
* **Narrative citation:** Use `\citet{Gomu2024}` $\rightarrow$ "Gomu et al. (2024)".
* **Parenthetical citation:** Use `\citep{Gomu2024}` $\rightarrow$ "(Gomu et al., 2024)".
* **Bibliography:**
    ```latex
    \bibliography{references}
    \bibliographystyle{iclr2025_conference}
    ```

## Figures and Tables
* All artwork must be neat, clean, and legible.
* **Captions:** Lower case (except for first word and proper nouns).
* **Placement:**
    * **Figures:** Caption appears **after** (below) the figure.
    * **Tables:** Caption appears **before** (above) the table.

## Math Notation
* ICLR encourages standardized notation using `\input{math_commands.tex}` (based on the Deep Learning book notation).
* Variables: Italics ($a$, $\va$, $\mA$).
* Random Variables: Roman ($P(\ra)$).
* Sets: Blackboard bold ($\R$, $\sA$).
* Functions: Standard LaTeX ($f(\vx)$).

references.text:
## Problem Statement
Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) have demonstrated significant capabilities in processing visual inputs; however, they suffer from a persistent issue known as object hallucination. This phenomenon occurs when models generate descriptions that inaccurately reflect visual content, either by including nonexistent objects or misrepresenting existing ones.

Our preliminary analysis suggests that two primary factors exacerbate this issue: (1) the presence of numerous irrelevant objects within a global image view disrupts the model's focus, and (2) low object resolution in full-image resizing impairs the model's ability to interpret fine-grained visual content. Existing mitigation strategies, such as data augmentation or instruction tuning, face scalability challenges. Meanwhile, current training-free methods often fail to fully exploit intrinsic visual information or rely on computationally expensive external modules. We require a mechanism that allows the model to dynamically concentrate on relevant high-resolution image regions during token generation without the need for additional training or external object detectors.

## Core Hypothesis
We propose that splitting a raw input image into multiple sub-images can mitigate hallucination by providing the model with views containing fewer distracting objects and higher resolution per object. However, simply processing all sub-images equally is inefficient and potentially noisy.

We hypothesize that the LVLM's internal attention mechanisms can serve as a dynamic guide. By monitoring the attention maps during the decoding process, we can identify which sub-image is most relevant to the current token being generated. We propose **Ensemble Decoding (ED)**, a training-free strategy that aggregates logit distributions from the original image and multiple sub-images, weighted by their real-time attention scores. This will allow the model to "zoom in" on necessary details dynamically, effectively utilizing intrinsic visual information to suppress hallucinations.

## Proposed Methodology (Detailed Technical Approach)

We will implement a framework consisting of three core components: Attention-Guided Weighting, Logit Ensembling, and an Adaptive Plausibility Constraint. Additionally, we will develop an optimized variant, FastED, for latency-sensitive applications.

### 1. Input Formulation and Image Splitting
We define a pre-trained LVLM as $p_{\theta}$ parameterized by $\theta$. Given a raw input image $v$ and text query $x$, we will split $v$ into $N$ sub-images, denoted as $v_1, v_2, \ldots, v_N \in \mathcal{R}^{c \times c}$. To ensure continuity and prevent object fragmentation at boundaries, we will resize images such that adjacent sub-images share overlapping regions. The model will process $N + 1$ distinct visual inputs (the original $v$ and the $N$ sub-images).

### 2. Attention-Guided Weight Calculation
At each decoding step $t$, we will calculate a weight for each sub-image based on the model's self-attention.
First, we compute the attention matrix $A_t$ using the query $Q_t$ and key $K_t$ matrices involving the text $x$, image $v$, and previously generated tokens $y_{<t}$:
$$ A_{t} = \mathrm{softmax} \left( \frac { Q_{t} K_{t}^{T} } { \sqrt { d_{k} } } \right) $$
where $d_k$ is the dimension of the key vectors.

To refine this matrix and reduce noise, we will average the attention scores from the top $K$ layers and the top $H$ heads within those layers. The refined attention matrix $\hat{A}_t$ of size $d \times d$ (number of patches) is defined as:
$$ \hat { A } _ { t } = \frac { 1 } { H } \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { H } \mathrm { sorted } \left( \frac { 1 } { K } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { K } \mathrm { sorted } ( A _ { t } ) [ i ] \right) [ j ] $$

We will then map the regions of $\hat{A}_t$ to our $N$ sub-images. We calculate the aggregated attention score $s_{k,t}$ for the $k$-th sub-image by summing the attention values in its corresponding region:
$$ s _ { k , t } = \sum _ { ( i , j ) \in \mathrm { Region } _ { k } } \hat { A } _ { t , i , j } \quad \mathrm { for } \quad k = 1 , 2 , \ldots , N $$

Finally, we convert these scores into normalized attention-guided weights $f_{k,t}$ using a softmax function with a temperature parameter $\tau$:
$$ f _ { k , t } = \frac { \exp ( s _ { k , t } / \tau ) } { \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { N } \exp ( s _ { j , t } / \tau ) } $$

### 3. Logit Ensemble
We will perform a forward pass for the global image and all sub-images. The final probability distribution for the token $y_t$ will be a weighted ensemble of the global logits and the sub-image logits. We introduce a weighting term $\alpha$ to balance the global and local context:
$$ P_{ED}(y_t | V, x, y_{<t}) = \mathrm{softmax} \left[ ( 1 - \alpha ) \mathrm { logit } _ { \theta } ( y _ { t } \mid v , x , y _ { < t } ) + \alpha \sum _ { k = 1 } ^ { N } \mathrm { logit } _ { \theta } ( y _ { t } \mid v _ { k } , x , y _ { < t } ) \cdot f _ { k , t } \right] $$
where $V$ denotes the set $\{v, v_{1:N}\}$.

### 4. ED Adaptive Plausibility Constraint
To ensure that the integration of probabilities from multiple images does not dilute fine-grained representations, we will implement a truncation mechanism. We define a set of valid tokens $\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{head}}$ based on a hyperparameter $\beta$. A token $y_t$ is retained only if its summed probability exceeds a fraction of the maximum weighted probability:
$$ \mathcal { V } _ { \mathrm { head } } ( y _ { < t } ) = \left\{ y _ { t } \in \mathcal { V } : \sum _ { k = 1 } ^ { N } p _ { \theta } ( y _ { t } \mid v _ { k } , x , y _ { < t } ) \geq \beta \operatorname* { max } _ { w } \left( \sum _ { k = 1 } ^ { N } p _ { \theta } ( w \mid v _ { k } , x , y _ { < t } ) \cdot f _ { k , t } \right) \right\} $$
Probabilities for tokens $y_t \notin \mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{head}}$ will be set to zero.

### 5. FastED Formulation
To address the computational cost of $N+1$ forward passes, we will develop **FastED**. This variant will dynamically select only the single sub-image $v_{k^*}$ with the highest attention-guided weight $f_{k^*}$ at step $t$. The ensemble equation reduces to:
$$ p _ { \mathrm { FastED } } ( y _ { t } \mid v , v _ { k ^ { * } } , x , y _ { < t } ) = \mathrm { softmax } \left[ ( 1 - \alpha ) \mathrm { logit } _ { \theta } ( y _ { t } \mid v , x , y _ { < t } ) + \alpha \cdot \mathrm { logit } _ { \theta } ( y _ { t } \mid v _ { k ^ { * } } , x , y _ { < t } ) \right] $$
This reduces the computational requirement to just 2 forward passes per token while maintaining the benefit of high-resolution local focus.

## Expected Contribution
1.  **Framework for Intrinsic Visual Exploitation:** We expect to demonstrate that LVLMs possess intrinsic, fine-grained visual knowledge that is often lost in global views. Our method will provide a theoretical and practical framework for recovering this information via attention maps.
2.  **State-of-the-Art Hallucination Mitigation:** By combining high-resolution sub-image logits with global context, we aim to achieve superior performance on hallucination benchmarks compared to existing training-free baselines.
3.  **Efficiency-Performance Balance:** The FastED variant will contribute a method that significantly reduces inference latency compared to full ensembling, offering a viable solution for real-time applications where precision is critical.
4.  **Module-Free Design:** Unlike methods requiring external object detectors or specific retraining, our approach will be purely decoding-based, ensuring broad applicability to various LVLM architectures that utilize patch-wise projectors.

preinstalled.en: python:3.11 bookworm; upstream code via PYTHONPATH; pdflatex + bibtex; CPU PyTorch with numpy, scipy, scikit-learn, pandas, matplotlib and more (pinned by constraints.txt)

notes.model: claude-opus-5-5 through the Anthropic Messages API (llm.provider=anthropic), no fallback models, reviewer model = same model. Requests carry model, messages and max_tokens only (no tools, no thinking parameter); ARC's per-stage temperature is not sent because the model rejects it, so the API default applies.
notes.agent: ARC is not a tool-using coding agent: its 23-stage pipeline, its own code agent and its reviewers are prompt chains over plain chat completions. conditions.agent=claude means only that the provider is Anthropic; Claude Code is not involved. Generated experiments run as a plain subprocess in the container.
notes.effort: ARC has no effort setting; usage-log.patch sends output_config.effort='high' with every request. Haiku 5.5 thinks by default and ARC's per-stage max_tokens (for example 4096) is shared with the thinking tokens, so long outputs can still be cut short.
notes.venue: Not chosen by the system: export.target_conference=iclr_2026 comes from [systems.autoresearchclaw].
notes.tokens: ARC records no usage. A logging-only patch (usage-log.patch) appends each Messages API `usage` block to anthropic-usage.jsonl; cost is not computed. The same patch carries the RWE_OMIT_TEMPERATURE and RWE_EFFORT switches.
notes.time: No global wall-clock or budget cap in ARC; only the runner's limit applies. Per experiment run 3600 s, refinement iterations 10, repair cycles 3.
notes.input: Chinese pack text goes verbatim (candidate files concatenated, with <!-- file --> markers) into prompts.extra_prompts of 18 stages. ARC takes one topic string and checks generated code against it, so research.topic is the candidate TASK.md verbatim with whitespace collapsed. Literature queries come from the stage-3 model plan; ARC's ASCII keyword splitter and its whitespace-based query expansion yield a few useless queries from the Chinese text. Starter papers are guidance text only: ARC cannot ingest seed papers.
notes.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: every request to api.anthropic.com is built in researchclaw/llm/anthropic_adapter.py:136-148 and carries only model, messages, max_tokens, optional temperature, output_config.effort and system, never a tools or web_search field; the OpenAI-compatible client (OpenRouter :online / plugins) is not used (llm.provider=anthropic), web_search.enabled=false, Gemini is only used by the disabled figure_agent.nano_banana. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so such a path would be invisible to the audit.
notes.secrets: Generated experiment code inherits the container environment, including the API keys (ARC offers no switch to scrub it).
notes.profile: project.profile=ml_generic is fixed for all tasks; research.domains is left empty because the literature screen rejects papers outside the stated domain (a theory task failed with domains=[machine-learning]).

preinstalled.en: upstream's locked dependencies (uv sync --frozen) plus compat.patch; TeX Live (with fonts-extra and latexmk); a research Python environment for the agent in /opt/research

notes.agent: No external coding agent: EvoScientist runs its own in-process planner/research/code/debug/writing sub-agents (LangChain deepagents) on the one configured model. conditions.agent only selects the provider; Claude Code and Codex are not used.
notes.model: Main agent, sub-agents and EvoScientist's auxiliary calls (tool selector, memory workers, summariser, graders) all use the configured model; auxiliary_model and model_fallbacks are empty.
notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. The execute shell and the EvoSkills paper-navigator scripts reach the world only through the shield; S2_DATE_CUTOFF is not set (the shield bounds dates).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: EvoScientist binds no provider-side search tool to any model (its only tools are think_tool, tavily_search when TAVILY_API_KEY is set, MCP tools from mcp.yaml, deepagents built-ins and skills; EvoScientist/EvoScientist.py:671-672 and 754-755 at the pin; the one bind_tools call is the tool selector's own output schema, middleware/tool_selector.py:166). TAVILY_API_KEY is not passed and the image has no mcp.yaml, so no search tool exists. Anthropic/OpenAI hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so a provider-side search would be invisible to the audit.
notes.credentials: The provider key is in the process environment and EvoScientist's execute shell inherits the environment (upstream has no switch); the key is therefore visible to the agent's shell. It is a run-scoped copy and is not logged by this adapter.
notes.memory: A fresh data dir per run (baked skills, empty memory). Memory workers, skill synthesis and the scheduler stay at upstream defaults, so their LLM calls count in the usage log.
notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.
